¶
'''boisterous''' (bois′tėr-ous), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''boystrous'', ''boustrous'', ''bowstrous'', ''boistrous''; < late ME. ''boistrous'', rough, coarse, a development, through the forms ''boisteous'', ''boystuous'', of the earlier form ''boistous'', which it has now superseded: see ''boistous''.] '''1†.''' Rough; coarse; stout; stiff.
{{smaller block|<poem>The leathern outside, ''boisterous'' as it was,
Gave way, and bent beneath her strict embrace.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Sigismonda and Guiscardo, l. 159.}}}}
'''2†.''' Rough and massive; bulky; cumbrous; clumsy.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''boystrous'' club, so buried in the grownd,
He could not rearen up againe so light.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 10.}}}}
'''3†.''' Rough in operation or action; violent; vehement. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The heat becomes too powerful and ''boisterous'' for them.
{{right|''Woodward'', Ess. towards a Nat. Hist. of the Earth.}}}}
'''4.''' Rough and stormy: applied to the weather, the waves, etc.—'''5.''' Exposed to the turbulence of the elements: as, a ''boisterous'' headland; a ''boisterous'' passage.—'''6†.''' Fierce; savage; truculent; full of violence: as, ''boisterous'' war.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Boist’rous'' Clifford, thou hast slain
The flower of Europe for his chivalry.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}}}
'''7.''' Turbulent; rough and noisy; clamorous: applied to persons or their actions: as, a ''boisterous'' man; ''boisterous'' merriment; a ''boisterous'' game.
{{smaller block|<poem>They love a captain to obey,
''Boisterous'' as March, yet fresh as May.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iii. 4.}}}}

[Native name.] The dog-headed boa, or ''Xiphosoma caninum'', a South American snake, family ''Boidæ'', notable for the beautiful green color of its skin. {{smaller|It is distinguished by having smooth scales, the marginal scales of the mouth pitted, and regular shields on the snout. Also called ''araramboya''.}}

'''bokark''' (bō′kärk), ''n.'' [Amer. Ind.] A basket of birch-bark, used by Lake Superior Indians to hold maple-sugar.

'''boke<sup>1</sup>''' (bōk), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''boked'', ppr. ''boking''. [E. dial., also ''buck''; in part a var. of ''poke'': see ''buck''<sup>4</sup> and ''poke''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To thrust; push; poke. [Eng.]

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To thrust; push; butt. ''Holland.''

'''boke<sup>2</sup>''', ''v.'' A dialectal form of ''bock'', ''bolk''.

'''bold†''' (bōld), ''v.'' [< ME. ''bolden'', ''balden'', tr. and intr., < AS. ''bealdian'', intr. be bold (= OHG. ''balden'', MHG. ''belden'', trans. make bold, = Goth. '''bole'''<sup>1</sup> (bōl), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''boal, boll''; < ME. ''bole'', < Icel. ''bolr, bulr'', trunk of a tree, = OSw. ''bol, bul'', Sw. ''bål'', a trunk, body, = Dan. ''bul'', trunk, stump, log, = MHG. ''bole'', G. ''bohle'', a thick plank; prob. akin, through the notion of roundness, to ''boll''<sup>1</sup>, ''bowl''<sup>1</sup>, ''ball''<sup>1</sup>, etc. ''Bole'' is the first element of ''bulwark'' and of its perversion ''boulevard'', q. v.] '''1.''' The body or stem of a tree.
{{smaller block|<poem>Huge trees, a thousand rings of Spring
In every ''bole''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, v.}}
The nerves of hearing clasp the roots of the brain as a creeping vine clings to the ''bole'' of an elm.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Old Vol. of Life, p. 271.}}}}
'''2.''' Anything of cylindrical shape; a roll; a pillar: as, ''boles'' of stone. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Make it up into little long ''boles'' or roules.
{{right|''True Gentlewoman’s Delight'' (1676).}}}}
'''3.''' A small boat suited for a rough sea. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Eng.]

{{smaller block|In the vigour of his physique, and an almost ''boisterous'' capacity for enjoyment, he was an English counterpart of the Scotch Christopher North. {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.''}}}}

'''boisterously''' (bois′tėr-us-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''boystrously''; < ''boisterous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''boistously''.]   In a boisterous manner; roughly; with noisy energy or activity.

<poem>When you come next to woo, pray you, come not ''boisterously'',
And furnish’d like a bear-ward.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Halloo’d it as ''boisterously'' as the rest.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iii. 20.}}}}

'''boisterousness''' (bois′tėr-us-nes), ''n.''   [< ''boisterous'' + ''-ness''.]   The state or quality of being boisterous; rough, noisy behavior; turbulence.

{{smaller block|Behaved with the ''boisterousness'' of men elated by recent authority. {{right|''Johnson'', Life of Prior.}}}}

'''boistous†''', ''a.''   [Early mod. E., also written ''boystous'', ''boisteous'', ''boysteous'', ''boistious'', ''boystuous'', etc., Sc. ''bousteous'', ''busteous'', etc.; < ME. ''boistous'', ''boystous'', ''buystous'', etc.; cf. mod. E. dial. (Cornwall) ''boustous'', ''boostis'', ''boustis'', ''bustious'', fat, corpulent, ''boist'', corpulence (perhaps a back-formation, from the adj.); origin unknown. The ME. agrees in form with AF. ''boistous'', OF. ''boisteus'', mod. F. ''boîteux'', lame, but no connection of sense is apparent. The W. ''bwystus'', wild, ferocious, is perhaps from E.]   '''1.''' Rude; rough; churlish; rustic; coarse: applied to persons. [The earliest recorded sense.]

{{smaller block|I am a ''boystous'' man, right thus say I.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Manciple’s Tale, l. 107.}}}}
{{smaller block|Myghte no blonkes [horses] theme bere, thos ''bustous'' churlles,
Bot coverde camellez of toures, enclosyde in maylez.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 615.}}}}
'''3.''' Rough and massive; bulky; clumsy. [Still in dial. use.]—'''4.''' Coarse in texture; rough; stout; thick.—'''5.''' Loud; violent; boisterous.

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To thrust; push; butt.   ''Holland.''

'''boke<sup>2</sup>''', ''v.'' A dialectal form of ''bock'', ''bolk''.

'''boke<sup>3</sup>''' (bōk), ''n.'' In ''mining'', a small run in pipes, found connecting the ore running through the vein.   ''R. Hunt.''

'''boke<sup>4</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''book''.

'''bokel†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''buckle''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bokeler†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''buckler''.

'''bolar''' (bō′lär), ''a.''   [< ''bole''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ar''.]   Pertaining to or of the nature of bole: as, ''bolar'' earths.

'''bolary†''' (bō′lạ-ri), ''a.''   [< ''bole''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ary'']   Pertaining to bole or clay, or partaking of its nature and qualities.
{{smaller block|Consisting of a ''bolary'' and clammy substance.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., ii. 3.}}}}

'''bolas<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''bullace''.

'''bolas<sup>2</sup>''' (bō′läs), ''n. sing.'' or ''pl.''   [Sp., pl. of ''bola'', a ball, < L. ''bulla'', a bubble, any round object: see ''bull''<sup>2</sup>, ''bill''<sup>3</sup>.]   A weapon of war and the chase, consisting of two or three balls of stone or metal attached to the ends of strong lines, which are knotted together, used by the Gauchos and Indians of western and southern South America. {{smaller|It is used by throwing it in such a way that the line winds around the object aimed at, as the legs of an animal. A smaller weapon of the same sort is in use among the Eskimos for killing birds.}}
{{smaller block|The ''bolas'', or balls, are of two kinds: the simplest, which is used chiefly for catching ostriches, consists of two round stones, covered with leather, and united by a thin, plaited thong, about eight feet long. The other kind differs only in having three balls united by thongs to a common centre. The Gaucho holds the smallest of the three in his hand, and whirls the other two around his head; then, taking aim, sends them like chain shot revolving through the air. The balls no sooner strike any object, than, winding round it, they cross each other and become firmly hitched. {{right|''Darwin'', Voyage of Beagle, iii. 50.}}}}

'''bolbonac†''', ''n.'' The satin-flower, ''Lunaria biennis.''

'''bold''' (bōld), ''a.''   [< ME. ''bold'', ''bald'', < AS. ''beald'', ''bald'' = OS. ''bald'' = D. ''boud'', bold (= MLG. ''balde'', ''bolde'', adv., quickly, at once), = OHG. ''bald'', MHG. ''balt'', bold (G. ''bald'', adv., soon), = Icel. ''ballr'' = ODan. ''bold'' = Goth. *''balths'', bold (in deriv. ''balthaba'', boldly, ''balthei'' = E. ''bield'', boldness, etc.). Hence ''bold'', ''v.'', ''bield'', ''n.'' and ''v.'', and (from OHG.) It. ''baldo'', OF. ''bald'', ''baud'', bold, gay: see ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Daring; courageous; brave; intrepid; fearless: applied to men or animals: as, ''bold'' as a lion.
{{smaller block|<poem>He has called him forty Marchmen ''bauld.''</poem>
{{right|''Kinmont Willie'', in Child’s Ballads, VI. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Our speech at best is half alive and cold,
And save that tenderer moments make us ''bold'',
Our whitening lips would close, their truest truth untold.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', To H. W. Longfellow.}}}}

'''2.''' Requiring or exhibiting courage; planned or executed with courage and spirit: as, a ''bold'' enterprise.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''bold'' design
Pleased highly those infernal States.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 386.}}}}

'''3†.''' Confident; trusting; assured.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am ''bold'' her honour
Will remain hers.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 4.}}}}

'''4.''' Forward; impudent; audacious: as, a ''bold'' huzzy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Men can cover crimes with ''bold'', stern looks.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1252.}}}}

'''5.''' Overstepping usual bounds; presuming upon sympathy or forbearance; showing liberty or license, as in style or expression: as, a ''bold'' metaphor.
{{smaller block|<poem>Which no ''bold'' tales of gods or monsters swell,
But human passions, such as with us dwell. {{right|''Waller.''}}</poem>
It is hardly too ''bold'' to claim the whole Netherlands as in the widest sense Old England.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 31.}}}}

'''6.''' Standing out to view; striking to the eye; markedly conspicuous; prominent: as, a ''bold'' headland; a ''bold'' handwriting.
{{smaller block|Catachreses and hyperboles are to be used judiciously, and placed in poetry, as heightenings and shadows in painting, to make the figure ''bolder'', and cause it to stand off to sight. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''7.''' Steep; abrupt: as, a ''bold'' shore (one that enters the water almost perpendicularly).
{{smaller block|Her dominions have ''bold'' accessible coasts. {{right|''Howell.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The coast [Virginia] is a ''bold'' and even coast, with regular soundings, and is open all the year round.
{{right|''Beverley'', Virginia, ii. ¶ 2.}}}}

'''8.''' Deep, as water, close to the shore; navigable very near to the land.
{{smaller block|The line [of soundings] was extended to Jacmel, showing ''bold'' water to the cape. {{right|''Science'', III. 591.}}}}

'''To be bold''' or '''so bold,''' to venture; presume so far (as to do something).
{{smaller block|<poem>Sir, let me ''be so bold'' as to ask you,
Did you yet ever see Baptista’s daughter?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will ''be bold'', since you will have it so,
To ask a noble favour of you.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''To make bold''', to take the liberty; use the freedom: as, I have ''made bold'' to call on you. ='''Syn. 1.''' Dauntless, doughty, valiant, manful, stout-hearted, intrepid, audacious, adventurous.—'''4.''' Saucy, impertinent, assuming, brazen-faced.}}

'''bold†''' (bōld), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bolden'', ''balden'', tr. and intr., < AS. ''bealdian'', intr. be bold (= OHG. ''balden'', MHG. ''belden'', trans. make bold, = Goth. ''balthjan'', intr. be bold, dare), < ''beald'', bold. Cf. ''bield'', ''v.'', a parallel form (< AS. ''byldan''), and ''embolden''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make bold; embolden; encourage.
{{smaller block|<poem>For this business,
It toucheth us, as France invades our land,
Not ''bolds'' the king.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become bold.
{{smaller block|<poem>For with that on encresede my fere,
And with that othir gan myn herte ''bolde''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 144.}}}}

'''bold-beating†''' (bōld′bē″ting), ''a.'' Browbeating: as, “''bold-beating'' oaths,” ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2.

'''bolden†''' (bōl′dn), ''v. t.''   [< ''bold'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''embolden''.]   To make bold; give confidence; encourage.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am much too venturous
In tempting of your patience; but am ''bolden’d''
Under your promis’d pardon.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 2.}}}}

'''bold-face''' (bōld′fās), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who has a bold face; an impudent person.
{{smaller block|A sauce-box, and a ''bold-face'', and a pert.
{{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, xix.}}}} '''2.''' In ''printing'', same as ''full-face''.

'''bold-faced''' (bōld′fāst), ''a.'' Having a bold face; impudent.
{{smaller block|The ''bold-faced'' atheists of this age.
{{right|''Bp. Bramhall'', Against Hobbes.}}}}

'''boldhead†''', ''n.''   [ME. ''boldhede''; < ''bold'' + ''head''.]   Boldness; courage.
{{smaller block|Ifallen is al his ''boldhede''.
{{right|''Owl and Nightingale'', l. 514.}}}}

'''boldine''' (bōl′din), ''n.''   [< ''boldo'' + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.]   An alkaloid extracted from the leaves of ''Peumus Boldus''. See ''boldo''.

'''boldly''' (bōld′li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''boldly'', ''boldliche'', etc., < AS. ''bealdlīce'', ''baldlīce'' (= OS. ''baldlīco'' = OHG. ''baldlīcho''), < ''beald'', bold.]   In a bold manner. {{smaller|(''a'') Courageously; intrepidly; fearlessly; bravely. (''b'') With confident assurance; without hesitation or doubt. (''c'') Vigorously; strongly; strikingly. (''d'') Impudently; insolently; with effrontery or shamelessness. (''e'') Steeply; abruptly; conspicuously.}}

'''boldness''' (bōld′nes), ''n.''   [< ''bold'' + ''-ness''. For the earlier noun, see ''bield''.]   The quality of being bold, in any of the senses of the word.
{{smaller block|Great is my ''boldness'' of speech toward you. 2 Cor. vii. 4.

''Boldness'' is the power to speak, or do what we intend, before others, without fear or disorder.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''boldness'' of the figures is to be hidden sometimes by the address of the poet, that they may work their effect upon the mind. {{right|''Dryden''.}}}}
{{smaller block|I cannot, with Johnson, interpret this word by fortitude or magnanimity. ''Boldness'' does not, I think, imply the firmness of mind which constitutes fortitude, nor the elevation and generosity of magnanimity. {{right|''N. Webster''.}}}}

'''boldo''' (bōl′dō), ''n.''   [Chilian.]   An aromatic evergreen shrub of Chili, ''Peumus Boldus'' (''Boldoa fragrans''), of the natural order ''Monimiaceæ''. {{smaller|The fruit of the plant is sweet and edible, and the bark is used for tanning. The leaves and bark are also used in medicine. See ''boldine''.}}

'''bole'''<sup>1</sup> (bōl), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''boal, boll''; < ME. ''bole'', < Icel. ''bolr, bulr'', trunk of a tree, = OSw. ''bol, bul'', Sw. ''bål'', a trunk, body, = Dan. ''bul'', trunk, stump, log, = MHG. ''bole'', G. ''bohle'', a thick plank; prob. akin, through the notion of roundness, to ''boll''<sup>1</sup>, ''bowl''<sup>1</sup>, ''ball''<sup>1</sup>, etc. ''Bole'' is the first element of ''bulwark'' and of its perversion ''boulevard'', q. v.]   '''1.''' The body or stem of a tree.
{{smaller block|<poem>Huge trees, a thousand rings of Spring

{{smaller block|The nerves of hearing clasp the roots of the brain as a creeping vine clings to the ''bole'' of an elm.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Old Vol. of Life, p. 271.}}}}
'''2.''' Anything of cylindrical shape; a roll; a pillar: as, ''boles'' of stone. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Make it up into little long ''boles'' or roules.
{{right|''True Gentlewoman’s Delight'' (1676).}}}}
'''3.''' A small boat suited for a rough sea.   ''Imp. Dict.'' [Eng.]
